title: FIFA to review impact of World Cup hydration breaks, Arsene Wenger says
content:
Arsene Wenger says FIFA will review the impact of hydration breaks on World Cup games after the tournament ends.

The introduction of hydration breaks at this summer’s tournament caused controversy, with many of the leading coaches at the World Cup speaking out against them.

Uruguay’s Marcelo Bielsa was one of their strongest critics, stating that the division of the game into quarters “adds nothing and takes away a lot”. The Athletic took an early look at how the breaks changed the momentum of games, but the results were inconclusive at that point.

Wenger was speaking at FIFA’s Technical Study Group’s closing press conference, heading up their group of tactical analysts as part of his role as chief of global football development.

He insisted that his team would study the data surrounding how hydration breaks have changed games throughout the tournament.

“Sometimes people didn’t like it. We will have to analyse after the World Cup, but it didn’t look to me as if they changed the outcome of the competition. In some games it was really needed,” he told reporters in New Jersey.

“Especially when the stadiums were covered, people were not happy with it, but at the start of the competition we made a decision to do it in every game so that there were no differences between games.

“We have not come to a conclusion yet but I promise that you will get one.”

Wenger and his team also faced questions on the logistics of the tournament, but played down the impact of travel distances and a lack of rest days on the quality of football played.

“The logistics of course were completely different, and before the tournament we were a bit anxious at FIFA that they could have an impact on the development of the game. I personally don’t share your view because I feel that we have had quality games here,” he added.

“Of course, in Qatar every night we slept in the same bed, not here. But again, when you see Argentina and Spain, the two teams have grown during the tournament, so the movement that they have had to do has not affected their performances.

“It’s always down to your quality and how much you want to win in the end. If you see the trophy and you think I want to take this trophy home, you accept a lot of suffering, and that is what has happened at this tournament.”
